topic: National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA) Collection
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Amrita Sher-Gil's 'Haldi Grinders' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted in 1940 at Saraya (Gorakhpur) using oil on canvas, 'Haldi Grinders' is one of the most poignant and celebrated mature masterpieces of Amrita Sher-Gil. Born to an Indian Sikh father and a Hungarian mother, Sher-Gil received elite academic training at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris before returning to India in 1934, declaring it her artistic destiny to interpret the life and silent melancholy of the Indian people. In 'Haldi Grinders', three rural women are depicted sitting upon the red earth under the shade of massive, curving tree trunks, grinding bright yellow turmeric using heavy stone pestles. Sher-Gil synthesizes European Post-Impressionism (Paul Gauguin) with the monumental dignity of Ajanta frescoes and the fiery color planes of Basohli miniatures. The glowing golden turmeric acts as an intense chromatic jewel against the deep terracotta red ground and dark tree trunks, capturing the silent endurance, tragic beauty, and timeless dignity of Indian village womanhood, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

topic: Democratization through Oleographs
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Raja Ravi Varma's 'Rama Vanquishing the Pride of the Ocean' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted around 1900 in oil on canvas by Raja Ravi Varma, 'Rama Vanquishing the Pride of the Ocean' is an epic landmark of modern Indian academic realism. Based on the Yuddha Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, the painting depicts Lord Rama standing upon dark, storm-tossed coastal rocks, fiercely aiming his celestial bow Kodanda with the fiery Agneyastra missile to evaporate the ocean after Varuna failed to grant passage to Lanka. Ravi Varma captures intense kinetic drama: Rama's red dhoti billows violently in the oceanic gale, while his powerful muscular stance radiates righteous fury. In the churning background, translucent green waves crash in frothing white surf against dark boulders, as the terrified ocean god Varuna rises with his entourage of sea nymphs with folded hands, pleading for divine mercy. Through the Ravi Varma Lithographic Press established in 1894, such dramatic mythological visions were mass-produced as color oleographs, transforming the visual consciousness of modern India, conserved in the Sri Chitra Art Gallery, Thiruvananthapuram.

topic: National Conservation Repository
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on P.V. Jankiram's 'Ganesha' and sheet metal sculpture and answer the questions that follow:

Created in 1970 using oxidized copper sheet metal, brass wires, and repoussé techniques, 'Ganesha' by P.V. Jankiram is a defining masterpiece of the 'Madras Movement' in modern Indian sculpture. Working at the Government College of Arts and Crafts in Madras and the Cholamandal Artists' Village under the mentorship of K.C.S. Paniker, Jankiram rejected both traditional stone carving and European academic bronze modeling. Instead, he drew inspiration from traditional South Indian temple craft, specifically 'Kavacham'—the sacred embossed sheet-metal casings placed over stone deities in sanctums. In 'Ganesha', Jankiram constructs a monumental, predominantly two-dimensional frontal sheet of oxidized copper. Across this planar surface, he solders delicate brass wires and textured metal strips to delineate Ganesha's crown, ears, trunk, and ornaments, while the deity gracefully plays a stringed veena, seamlessly fusing traditional temple ritual craft with modern linear constructivism, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

topic: Ethical and Humanist Status
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Somnath Hore's 'Children' and the 'Wounds' series and answer the questions:

Created around 1970 by master sculptor and printmaker Somnath Hore, 'Children' from the celebrated 'Wounds' series is one of the most heartbreaking and ethically uncompromising humanist statements in modern world art. Hore's artistic consciousness was indelibly shaped by his firsthand witness of human agony during the man-made 1943 Bengal Famine and the 1946 Tebhaga peasant uprising. In 'Children', Hore abandoned conventional ink and printing presses entirely, pioneering his radical technique of casting raw, wet paper pulp directly onto a scarred cement matrix. The resulting artwork is an inkless, pure white-on-white relief: the raised paper pulp presents gashes, scars, and skeletal, hollowed contours of starving infants. Hore deliberately refused to use color, asserting that pretty colored inks would only decorative-ize and betray the raw, unadorned tragedy of human suffering, conserved in the NGMA, New Delhi.

topic: Color Palette of Gossip
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on N.S. Bendre's 'Gossip' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted in 1969 in oil on canvas, 'Gossip' by Narayan Shridhar (N.S.) Bendre is a radiant, luminous triumph of post-independence Indian figurative modernism. Bendre, who played an instrumental role in shaping the modern visual pedagogy of the Faculty of Fine Arts at M.S. University of Baroda, employed a personalized adaptation of Pointillism and Divisionism to capture the dazzling brilliance of Indian sunlight. In 'Gossip', three rural women clad in vibrant sarees of warm marigold yellow, vermilion red, and magenta are seated intimately together in an enclosure of shared confidences. Bendre simplifies their bodies and facial features into broad, harmonious color planes without academic photographic detailing, letting the tilt of their heads, the angle of their shoulders, and the warmth of the glowing daylight convey their lively village camaraderie, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi.
